recent.say: I back I39’s free pilot: four families completing a second challenge is a measurable hurdle. That earns a test, not a business valuation.
Lukas, agreed on convenience. At the carpentry shop, I’d compare minutes spent booking both ways, including failed deliveries. A higher price needs measurable time saved.
For I39, are we designing for home or museum visits? I suggest testing at-home play first, so returning doesn’t require another family outing.
I oppose I36 for production now: we still have no observed repeat use from couriers. I can seek delivery-operator introductions through the coworking space.
🎧 For I44, does the loop find and check gigs itself, or am I secretly curating every evening? Which exceptions actually need me?
The tax-relief notice gives us a deadline, not a recurring product. I need evidence of regularly changing benefits before pitching a one-screen eligibility feed.
Kristaps, agreed: count failed-delivery time too. I’m not backing I36 yet; sixteen classmates aren’t repeat users, and recruitment still has no owner.
Guys, listen, for I42 let’s test whether transport questions actually repeat: ask two receptionists to tally a week’s questions and handling minutes before we build daily cards.
For I41, who actually pays the proposed €3: organisers or suppliers passing it on? ✨ How would we reach the first ten paying organisers this week?
The holiday closures suggest a useful one-week alert, not a new recurring business. Before pitching another feed, I’d audit seven days of notices for genuinely new, actionable changes.
I38 has to beat simply picking up litter on a normal walk. I’ll test that comparison before defending a mission feed; I’m withholding support for I36.

I’m not backing I36 without repeat use. Lukas, test I43 for €0: ask two providers to quote one delivery route with your proposed €3 fee deducted. If neither accepts the margin, skip the matching machine 😅.
I back I39’s free test: completing a second challenge means more than saving a link. I’m keeping my all-in card until couriers actually return.
For I44, do students want daily picks or only weekend plans? Ask ten SSE students about their last concert search before choosing the delivery frequency.
Let me push back: I36 needs no recruitment platform. Approach couriers outside takeaways, with permission, and test two checked briefings before building anything.

recent.say: I oppose I38 for now: missions haven't shown value beyond an ordinary cleanup walk. What runs without us, and which safety checks still need a human?

For I39, let parents report completion without uploading children’s photos. We need evidence of repeat play, not a collection of family living rooms.
I back I39’s free pilot: a challenge parents and kids actually finish together beats another saved activity link. Let’s test repeat play, not clicks. ⚽
I’ll take I36 recruitment this week: ask takeaway staff permission, then invite couriers between orders. Their break is NOT free research time; keep it optional and brief.

risks: The supplied notice does not establish comprehensive or continuing roadworks coverage.
Four unsolicited requests could indicate interest without demonstrating safer journeys, time savings or willingness to pay.

Collecting contact details creates avoidable privacy obligations; use explicit opt-in, minimal records and a clear deletion date.

lastWeeklyReview.milestone: Within seven days, a human approaches ten couriers while they are stationary, records consent and current information methods, and offers two independently checked briefings for one affected area. Bound the experiment to €0 incremental cash spending and four total person-hours, including checking; stop if either bound cannot be met. Define return beforehand as a distinct participant requesting another briefing without a reminder within 48 hours o
dissent: A free, tightly scoped briefing may merit testing before a payer is identified because repeat-use behavior can cheaply challenge the usefulness hypothesis.
Human checking may be an appropriate permanent safety control; full autonomy need not be the goal if measured operating effort remains acceptable.

lastWeeklyReview.risk: Managers may request convenient quotes while providers reject the €3 fee, leaving apparent interest without a viable payer.
risks: Free self-collection or directly arranged delivery may be preferable to an intermediary.
Unverified collection eligibility, quantities and availability could make quoted deliveries infeasible.
Coordination, cancellations and disputes could consume the proposed fee.
Daily matching is only a proposed workflow; supplier confirmations and human oversight remain necessary.
evidenceGaps: Managers' delivery frequency, quantities, urgency and willingness to pay an all-in delivery price.
Providers' willingness to accept the €3 completion fee and their underlying delivery costs.
Current collection rules, eligibility and practical collection arrangements.
Comparable direct-delivery prices and the cost of human coordination.
No customer contact, tests, payments or implementation have occurred.
lastWeeklyReview.milestone: Within seven days and €20 total discovery spend, a human invites ten Riga property managers and interviews at least three prospective delivery providers. Show managers verified self-collection conditions and itemized, nonbinding delivery quotes. Pass only if at least three managers request a dated quote specifying quantity and address area, and at least two providers state in writing that they would accept the proposed €3 fee per completed delive
dissent: Free sand could strengthen a convenience proposition because the remaining problem may be transport rather than material cost.
A small manual pilot may reveal enough coordination value to justify a provider fee; paying customers are not required merely to investigate that hypothesis.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

principles.title: A signal is not a customer
principles.text: Use dated source receipts. Keep contextual signals, hypotheses and real validation separate. Agreement among fictional roles is not corroboration.

principles.title: Give someone a reason to return
principles.text: Name a reachable audience, a real recurring problem or delight, and what they receive every week.

principles.title: Know the payer and the alternatives
principles.text: Treat the price as a hypothesis until a real test. Include existing alternatives, acquisition, fees, refunds and human minutes. A justified free test is allowed.

principles.title: Bound the whole loop
principles.text: Specify trigger, make, separate check, deliver and exception owner. Tool documentation proves capability, not demand or successful operation.

principles.title: Try to disprove it cheaply
principles.text: Write a human-runnable test with explicit pass/fail thresholds before expanding the build. A plan is not implementation.

records.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
records.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

candidate.payerAndPrice: Hypothesis: the owner or manager pays €25/month per hotel. Recruit through permission-based invitations, not guest lists. Test usefulness free before asking decision-makers about price; interest is not payment or validated demand.
candidate.valueProposition: Hypothesis: a dated, narrowly scoped transport card reduces repeated arrival-answer work without sacrificing accuracy. The supplied bus notice demonstrates changing route information, not hotel demand, complete journey coverage or current conditions.
candidate.firstTest: Propose a €0, non-guest-facing comparison within seven days: two receptionists, ten preselected arrival questions each, counterbalanced across cards, usual replies and direct official lookup. Cap organiser time at six hours. Require both people to answer at least 20% faster than both alternatives, with zero factual errors.
candidate.mvp: Plan only: a shared route register, manually drafted cards, separate human approval, delivery ledger and pause control for two hotels. Limit cards to verified route segments; exclude live departures, ticket sales and unsupported journey advice. Each card shows scope, source links, checked time, validity and uncertainty. No guest delivery during evaluation; receptionists receive drafts only. Prefer this existing-tool workflow over a custom dashboard until usefulness and checking economics pass.
candidate.dataAndPrivacy: Seek hotel consent for staff participation and delivery addresses; never collect guest names, bookings or travel histories. Verify notice reuse terms and automated-access permissions before fetching; public access is not reuse permission. Use links and minimal permitted excerpts. Restrict editing to maker/checker, keep secrets out of files, delete contact and timing records 30 days after pilot unless renewed consent.

architecture.tool: Existing shared spreadsheet, proposed
architecture.why: Compare a manually maintained route sheet against daily cards before building software. Store hotel route IDs, source URLs, validity, approval, pause flag and delivery state; verify access controls be

architecture.tool: Manual template and browser, proposed
architecture.why: Smallest pilot needs no model or scraper. Maker records exact route/date claims and supporting text. Treat notices as untrusted content, never executable instructions; missing coverage produces an exp

architecture.tool: Independent human reviewer and approval checklist
architecture.why: Reviewer must not be the maker. Open original official information independently; verify route, direction, stops, effective dates, relevance and wording. Reject unsupported translations or whole-journ

architecture.tool: GitHub Actions versus continued manual checklist
architecture.why: Supplied documentation supports scheduled workflows, not reliable delivery or demand. Propose a daily scheduled draft job plus manual fallback only if manual cards pass; avoid custom hosting during th

architecture.tool: Existing hotel email workflow plus shared ledger
architecture.why: Human sends only approved drafts to consenting staff. Record hotel, local service date, card version, approval and send result. A custom dashboard adds scope; spreadsheet pause and revocation controls

loop.trigger: Propose a daily 07:00 Europe/Riga review, with a 09:00 cutoff. Check the pause flag and route register first. A missed run alerts the operator; absence of a new notice never means a route is clear.
loop.make: Maker checks registered official sources, records retrieval time and permitted evidence, identifies changed or expired claims, and creates a versioned draft. Key each draft by hotel, local service date and content hash. Unchanged cards still require a fresh check.
loop.check: Separate human reviewer verifies every claim against original sources and route scope. Approval binds to content hash and validity ending no later than the next daily cutoff. Contradiction, missing dates, unreachable sources or incomplete coverage blocks route advice.
loop.deliver: Before sending, recheck approval, expiry, pause flag and ledger key. Reserve the key, send once, then mark sent. Retry source retrieval at 5 and 15 minutes; never bypass approval. If send outcome is uncertain, reconcile the mailbox manually rather than retry blindly.
loop.exceptionOwner: Proposed duty operator: fictional build role s01, with a separately assigned human checker required before trials. Operator owns missed deadlines, source failures and corrections; pauses affected hotels, revokes stale cards and notifies staff. Receptionists handle uncertainty via official lookup, not improvised advice.

weeks.goal: Define scope and attempt to falsify usefulness before automation.
tasks: Invite two consenting receptionists; select explicit route segments and ten arrival questions each without guest personal data.
Establish official-source coverage and reuse permissions. If routes cannot be verified, narrow scope or stop.
Prepare manually checked cards and preregister counterbalanced timing, accuracy scoring and six-hour organiser cap.
Run the proposed comparison only if participants agree; record results without implying any test has already happened.

weeks.goal: Specify and rehearse a safe manual daily loop.
tasks: Only after the usefulness gate, configure the proposed spreadsheet, card template, approval fields, ledger and pause control.
Assign different maker and checker; require explicit route, direction, dates, source and expiry checks.
Rehearse missing sources, expired notices, unrelated notices and unsupported route coverage using labelled simulations.
Compare daily cards with maintaining a single route sheet; retain the simpler alternative if equally useful.

weeks.goal: Evaluate reliability and labour without guest exposure.
tasks: Propose five daily staff-only rehearsals; log maker, checker, exception and hotel-specific minutes.
Inject duplicate triggers, send timeouts, altered approved content and a paused hotel; verify blocking and reconciliation.
If justified, draft a GitHub Actions schedule configuration and manual fallback; deployment is not required for the MVP.
Require current source verification each day; label gaps and invalidate expired cards rather than recycling advice.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to stop, simplify or propose a paid pilot.
tasks: Review timing, factual accuracy, daily labour and incident logs against preregistered gates.
Ask each hotel's budget holder about the explicit €25/month offer, cancellation terms and purchasing process; record refusals.
Estimate acquisition, onboarding, review, support, tax, refunds and supplier costs before proposing payment collection.
Do not launch if accuracy or coverage fails. Prefer the route sheet if it matches benefits; propose a separately consented paid pilot only if gates pass.

economics.hypothesis: At a proposed €25/month, ten hypothetical hotels yield €250/month gross before tax, fees and refunds. No conversion, traffic or revenue is established. Shared review across hotels is necessary to test, not assume.
economics.costAssumptions: Illustrative assumptions: €15/hour labour, 30 review days, five shared review minutes/day, two support minutes/hotel/month and €10/month tools. At ten hotels, costs total €52.50/month before acquisition, onboarding, payment fees, refunds and tax. Supplier's $5 paid hosting minimum is not a euro quote.
economics.unitEconomics: Under those assumptions, €250 minus €52.50 leaves €197.50/month before excluded costs. At only two hotels, the same shared workload leaves €1.50/month before exclusions. Five extra hotel-specific minutes/day cost €37.50/hotel/month, exceeding the proposed price.
unknowns: Actual shared versus hotel-specific checking minutes and weekend coverage.
Acquisition time, conversion, retention, onboarding and willingness to pay.
Payment fees, VAT treatment, refunds, currency conversion and tool-plan limits.
Whether reduced answering time is worth more than the subscription and staff handling burden.

tests.hypothesis: Checked cards outperform both existing replies and direct official lookup.
tests.test: Human-run, staff-only comparison: two receptionists answer ten questions each in counterbalanced conditions. Independent reviewer scores route/date accuracy; record answer times and unsupported answers.
tests.pass: Both receptionists have at least 20% lower median answer time versus each alternative; every card-assisted answer is factually correct and within verified scope.
tests.fail: Any factual error, unsupported answer, either participant below the speed threshold, or inability to verify relevant routes. Missing recruitment leaves the hypothesis untested.

tests.hypothesis: The loop blocks unsafe and duplicate delivery with affordable labour.
tests.test: Human-run rehearsal over five days, plus ten labelled fault cases covering stale dates, absent coverage, source failure, modified approval, duplicate triggers and ambiguous email outcomes.
tests.pass: All unsafe sends blocked; zero duplicates; all exceptions assigned and acknowledged before cutoff. Shared review averages at most five minutes/day and hotel-specific support at most two minutes/month equivalent.
tests.fail: Any unsafe or duplicate send, unowned exception, or labour above the proposed economic budget. Small samples do not prove production reliability.

tests.hypothesis: A hotel budget holder sees enough value to consider €25/month.
tests.test: After usefulness testing, a human presents both managers with scope, limitations, €25/month price and cancellation terms; ask for a specific, non-binding paid-pilot decision and reason.
tests.pass: Both identify purchasing authority and at least one requests a dated paid-pilot proposal at €25/month. Treat this only as price interest, not validated revenue.
tests.fail: Neither requests a proposal, price exceeds perceived savings, or no budget authority can be identified; revise or stop. Actual willingness to pay remains unproven without payment.

risks: Daily review can miss intraday changes; cards must state checked time, limited scope and expiry, never promise disruption-free travel.
A municipal route notice does not establish complete airport, station or hotel journey coverage.
Separate human review can still miss errors; critical uncertainty must block advice rather than produce confident wording.
Manual delivery lacks transactional guarantees; ambiguous sends require reconciliation, not automatic resending.
Daily checker availability, language verification and hotel-specific exceptions may make €25/month uneconomic.
unknowns: Which selected routes have sufficient official coverage and permission for the proposed use?
How many relevant questions occur, and are existing replies already accurate and quick?
Which languages are essential, and who can independently verify them?
Will hotels prefer daily cards, change-only updates or an ordinary route sheet?
Who will cover checker absence, weekends and urgent corrections before any guest-facing pilot?

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: Cloudflare Workers official pricing
evidence.excerpt: The Workers Paid plan includes Workers, Pages Functions, Workers KV, Hyperdrive, and Durable Objects usage for a minimum charge of $5 USD per month for an account. The plan includes increased initial usage allotments, with clear charges for usage that exceeds the base plan. There are no additional charges for data transfer (egress) or throughput (bandwidth). ## Workers Users on the Workers Paid plan have access to the Standard usage model. Workers Enterprise accounts are billed based on the usage model specified in their contract. To switch to the Standard usage model, contact your Account Manager. | | Requests 1, 2, 3, 4 | Duration | CPU time | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Free** | 100,000 per day | No charge for duration | 10 milliseconds of CPU time per invocation | | **Standard** | 10 million included per month +$0.30 per additional million | No charge or limit for duration | 30 million CPU milliseconds included per month +$0.02 per additional million CPU milliseconds Max of [5 minutes of CPU time](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#account-plan-limits) per invocation (default: 30 seconds) Max of 15 minutes of CPU time per [Cron Trigger](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/) or [Queue Consumer](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer) invocation | 1 Inbound requests to your Worker. Cloudflare does not bill for [subrequests](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#subrequests) you make from your Worker. 2 WebSocket connections made to a Worker are charged as a request, representing the initial `Upgrade` connection made to establish the WebSocket. WebSocket messages routed through a Worker do not count as requests. 3 Requests to static assets are free and unlimited. 4 When [Workers Caching](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/cache/) is enabled, requests served from the Worker's cache are billed at the same per-request rate as requests that invoke the Worker. This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). CPU time is only billed when the Worker runs (on a cache miss or bypass).

hypotheses: Managers without convenient collection transport, potentially those managing multiple properties, experience repeated winter replenishment problems and value dated deliveries.
Providers could pay €3 per completed delivery if incremental order margin exceeds the fee and coordination costs; neither the price nor that margin is validated.

Proposed €20 discovery test: invite ten Riga property managers, compare verified free self-collection conditions and directly arranged delivery with the proposed service, and require at least three dated quote requests specifying quantity and address area.

Separately approach at least three prospective providers; require at least two written, nonbinding acceptances of the hypothetical €3 completion fee alongside itemized delivery prices. These thresholds test stated interest, not paid demand. No outreach or tests have occurred.
unknowns: Collection eligibility for managers and third-party couriers, collection locations, limits, stock and practical arrangements.
Actual replenishment frequency, quantities, urgency, existing collection methods and willingness to pay an all-in delivery price.
Provider availability, direct-delivery alternatives, delivery costs and willingness to accept the completion fee.
Acquisition costs, cancellations, refunds, disputes and human coordination minutes per order; no evidence supports daily matching volume.
dissent: Free municipal sand could strengthen a transport-convenience proposition, but managers may already collect it cheaply or use existing contractors.
Manager quote requests alone would not validate the provider-funded model; providers could prefer direct orders without an intermediary fee.
reports.question: Who experiences this recurring problem, who could pay, and which precise source signal supports that hypothesis? Separate EU aggregate context from Riga evidence.

candidate.audience: Hypothesis: Riga property managers who lack convenient transport for pavement sand, initially in one delivery area chosen after provider interviews. The municipal receipt supports free sand availability, not demand for delivery or daily orders.
candidate.payerAndPrice: Hypothesis: delivery providers pay €3 per completed, undisputed delivery. Managers pay the provider's disclosed all-in delivery price directly. Obtain written fee acceptance before any proposed pilot; quote requests alone do not validate the payer.
candidate.valueProposition: Proposed convenience: obtain a dated, itemized delivery option without separately coordinating collection and transport. Compare against verified eligible free self-collection and directly arranged delivery. Do not promise municipal collection access until third-party collection rules are checked.
candidate.firstTest: Within seven days, a human would invite ten managers and interview at least three providers, spending at most €20 total. Show verified self-collection terms and nonbinding delivery options. Pass only with three dated quote requests specifying quantity and area, plus two written provider acceptances of the hypothetical €3 completion fee.
candidate.mvp: Plan only; nothing has been built, tested or sold. Propose a four-week concierge pilot: one area, one request form, restricted order ledger, manual provider matching and independent human checking. No app, routing engine, inventory promises or payment integration. Track request → checked quote → manager approval → provider acceptance → delivery confirmation → disputed/complete. Expand only after discovery gates pass.
candidate.dataAndPrivacy: Propose collecting business contact, area, quantity, date and sharing permission; request exact address only when needed for quoting. Share details only with an explicitly authorized provider; no public ledger or door codes. s30 edits operations; s03 checks and approves; s19 receives redacted research. Use restricted accounts, MFA and an access log. Delete unsuccessful inquiries after 30 days; confirm lawful invoice retention separately.

architecture.tool: Proposed existing form and restricted spreadsheet
architecture.why: Compare manual form/spreadsheet handling against custom software using synthetic cases first. Choose existing tools if permissions and audit needs pass review; no custom marketplace is justified by cu

architecture.tool: Manual calendar reminder; GitHub Actions as an alternative
architecture.why: Start with a human reviewing the ledger at 09:00 Europe/Riga. Supplied documentation supports scheduled workflows, not reliable delivery operations. Consider a scheduler only after repeated manual omi

architecture.tool: s03 checklist and protected approval columns
architecture.why: s30 drafts matches; s03 independently checks source freshness, collection permission, quantity, availability, total price, fee disclosure and delivery window. No quote is released without recorded app

architecture.tool: Request IDs, duplicate key and append-only event log
architecture.why: Propose a normalized contact + address + date + quantity key. Flag repeats for human merge, not automatic deletion. One active provider assignment per request; log quote version, approval and message

architecture.tool: Cloudflare Workers versus no custom backend
architecture.why: The supplied minimum paid-plan cost is $5/month, not evidence that hosting is needed. Defer custom hosting until manual workflow volume and economics justify maintenance; obtain current tool and curre

loop.trigger: Proposed daily 09:00 Europe/Riga review of new and unresolved requests; urgent requests get no guaranteed response. Empty queue means no matching or promotional messages. s30 checks missed runs manually.
loop.make: s30 deduplicates, assigns an ID and seeks itemized quotes from authorized providers. Record quantity, material source, collection rights, delivery window, taxes, handling, total price and quote expiry. Never infer stock from the municipal announcement.
loop.check: s03 independently verifies collection eligibility and same-day availability with the relevant source/provider, arithmetic, permissions and quote version. Missing evidence blocks release. Manager approves total and window; provider then explicitly accepts the assignment.
loop.deliver: Send the checked offer through the manager's agreed channel. After acceptance, share only necessary delivery details. Request provider completion and manager acknowledgment; absent acknowledgment remains pending. Record a single fee event only after undisputed completion, subject to agreed terms.
loop.exceptionOwner: s30 owns exceptions; s03 handles disputes involving s30. Retry unanswered quotes once after four business hours; after one business day, notify the manager and expire or seek an approved alternative. Never rebook an uncertain delivery. Freeze fees on disputes; obtain fresh approval for substitutions, changed prices or dates.

weeks.goal: Disprove demand and payer assumptions before building.
tasks: s19 would verify municipal eligibility, third-party collection, quantities, locations and practical availability; record dated evidence and unresolved conditions.
s30 would run the €20 manager/provider discovery test, comparing self-collection and direct delivery without claiming bookings or demand.
s03 would review consent wording, itemized quote templates and written fee acceptance. Stop or revise if either discovery threshold fails.

weeks.goal: Prepare and dry-run the smallest operational workflow.
tasks: If discovery passes, configure the proposed form, restricted ledger, statuses, permissions, IDs and quote versioning; otherwise continue interviews without building.
Run ten synthetic cases including duplicate intake, stale stock, price change, provider silence, lost message and disputed completion.
Compare existing-tool handling with a paper/manual baseline; retain the simplest option meeting checker, privacy and audit requirements.

weeks.goal: Conditionally attempt a tightly bounded human-run pilot.
tasks: Only after permissions, collection rules and terms are verified, invite up to five consenting requests in one area; promise quotes, not guaranteed deliveries.
s30 would match manually; s03 must approve each released quote. Require manager approval and provider acceptance before booking.
Log handling minutes, response times, direct alternatives, cancellations and unresolved outcomes. No deliveries, users or revenue are claimed to have occurred.

weeks.goal: Review feasibility and choose stop, revise or continue.
tasks: Reconcile any proposed pilot outcomes with both sides; separate quote requests, bookings, completed deliveries, fee invoices and collected revenue.
Review duplicate prevention, missed reminders, retries, privacy access and disputes using synthetic cases where real cases are absent.

Calculate contribution including human time. Continue only if demand and payer gates pass and observed costs suggest a credible path below €3 per completion; otherwise change price, narrow scope or stop.

economics.hypothesis: A €3 provider fee could work only if incremental provider margin and coordination value exceed the fee. Neither provider acceptance nor manager willingness to pay delivery costs is validated.
economics.costAssumptions: Planning assumptions: €20 discovery cap; €0 incremental existing-tool spend if permitted accounts suffice; labor valued at €12/hour. Optional Workers paid hosting starts at supplied $5/month, with currency, tax and usage costs to verify. No platform-funded delivery subsidy.
economics.unitEconomics: Illustration, not forecast: €3 fee less five minutes at €12/hour leaves €2 before acquisition, tools, tax, refunds and disputes. At 15 minutes, labor alone consumes €3. A €20 acquisition spend spread over ten completed orders would add €2/order; ten completions are hypothetical.
unknowns: Provider margin after fuel, loading, material, travel and the proposed fee.
Completion rate, repeat demand, seasonal volume and acquisition cost.
Coordination minutes, fee collection cost, taxes, disputes and cancellations.
Whether providers would pay an invoiced fee rather than bypass the service.

tests.hypothesis: Managers want delivery quotes and providers accept the proposed payer model.
tests.test: Human invites ten managers and interviews at least three providers; compares verified self-collection and direct delivery. Share one €20 discovery budget.
tests.pass: At least three dated quote requests with quantity and area, and two written nonbinding acceptances of €3 per completed delivery.
tests.fail: Either threshold is missed, or feasible collection rights and delivery terms cannot be verified. Interest is not paid validation.

tests.hypothesis: Existing tools can support a safe, independently checked daily loop.
tests.test: Human runs ten synthetic cases, including duplicates, retries, changed prices, stale availability and uncertain completion; compare against a manual checklist.
tests.pass: Zero duplicate assignments or fees; every outgoing quote has independent approval; all blocked cases reach the named owner.
tests.fail: Any unchecked release, unauthorized disclosure, duplicate booking or orphaned exception; fix and rerun before a live pilot.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed fee can cover coordination without hiding delivery costs.
tests.test: Conditionally offer up to five consenting pilot requests; time all handling and compare itemized direct-delivery alternatives. Do not subsidize fulfillment.
tests.pass: At least three undisputed completions, corresponding €3 fees actually collected under agreed terms, and mean handling time at most five minutes per completion.
tests.fail: Thresholds unmet within four weeks, including insufficient requests; distinguish inconclusive volume from operational failure. No automation expansion.

risks: Free collection or directly arranged delivery may be preferable; the municipal receipt does not validate demand.
Third-party collection may be restricted; stop affected quotes until permission is verified.
Weather, stock, load limits and unsafe unloading can make accepted windows infeasible; do not promise emergency pavement safety.
The €3 fee may be consumed by labor, acquisition and disputes; providers may bypass the intermediary.
Business contacts and delivery addresses still require controlled access, appropriate processing terms and retention review.
unknowns: Current collection eligibility, stock, limits and authorization for couriers.
Reachable provider coverage, insurance, safe handling and cancellation terms.
Manager replenishment frequency and actual preference versus existing contractors.
Appropriate legal role, invoicing, liability and data-processing arrangements.

loop.check: Separate checker s29 verifies claims, dates, place, rights, pronunciation, duration and final audio against the approved script. Track source yield, rejection reasons, checker availability and production minutes; do not weaken standards to fill slots.

Collect voluntary repeat reports using the same definition; report nonresponses and distinguish new from returning listeners.

tasks: Compare repeat reports, source yield, failures, cash and total human time across weeks.

economics.hypothesis: A founder-funded free pilot may earn another experiment if repeat listening and operational controls pass. Proposed four-week cash ceiling: €50, including week one's €20. No revenue or cost recovery is established.
economics.costAssumptions: Assume existing devices/accounts and €0 incremental recording expense; verify hosting terms before use. No paid acquisition or listening rewards. Value all team time at a hypothetical €15/hour. Recruitment and permissions count toward the six-hour first-test cap. At €0, no payment fees or refunds are planned.
economics.unitEconomics: Scenario: three episodes and six team hours imply €90 labor plus up to €20 cash, or €110 total and €36.67 per episode. With exactly four repeat listeners, that is €27.50 per repeat listener. Revenue would be €0. These are planning calculations, not observed performance.
unknowns: Actual recruitment cost and human minutes per approved episode.
Permission fees, service charges, storage costs and enough suitable daily sources.
Listener willingness to pay, sponsor purchasing authority, acquisition cost and acceptable editorial boundaries.

tests.hypothesis: At least four of ten commuters voluntarily return for a distinct episode.
tests.test: A human recruits ten consenting commuters and offers three checked episodes on fixed days within seven days. Each gets a 48-hour response window and identical availability notices, not individual reminders. Optional reports identify episodes played; no reward for listening.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

plan.audience: Hypothesis: Riga NGO organisers arranging repeated small catered events, initially ten organisers reachable through moderator-approved local groups. Municipal reuse guidance supplies context, not evidence of sourcing pain or customer demand.
plan.payerAndPrice: Hypothesis: the organiser controlling the event budget pays €3 per completed rental for assisted coordination, separately from supplier rental, deposit, cleaning and transport charges. Disclose the fee before measuring interest. No payments are proposed during the first test.
plan.valueProposition: Proposed benefit: receive dated, quantity-checked tableware options with explicit cleaning, collection and return terms. Compare assisted coordination against contacting the same suppliers directly and using venue tableware; do not assume the intermediary adds value.
plan.firstTest: Within seven days and €20 total, seek permission for two supplier listings and verify their full terms. Invite ten NGO organisers through permitted groups. Show direct and assisted options with €3 disclosed. Pass if three distinct organisers request real dated quotes and at least two choose assistance at that fee; otherwise revise or stop.
plan.mvp: Plan only; nothing has been contacted, tested or implemented. Use a private spreadsheet, consent form and manually sent email for two permissioned listings and ten organisers. Track requests, dated inventory, checks, quote versions and status. A separate human checker gates every quote. Suppliers confirm reservations; no instant booking, payment processing, public marketplace or delivery service. Proceed beyond discovery only if the first test passes.
plan.dataAndPrivacy: Obtain supplier permission for each listed field and organiser permission before sharing contact details with a named supplier. Store dates, quantities, area and contact email; avoid guest data. Restrict the ledger to assigned team roles; keep contacts out of code/logs. Propose deletion 30 days after closure, subject to necessary dispute retention. Confirm provider terms and access controls before use.

architecture.why: Prefer a human-operated existing-tool workflow over a custom marketplace. Evaluate permissions and export/deletion settings before selection. Separate Contacts, Listings, Requests, Holds, Checks and O

architecture.tool: Separate checker worksheet and human sign-off
architecture.why: Propose s09 as preparer and s20 as checker. Require a quote-version-specific approval with source confirmation timestamps. A preparer cannot approve their own quote; an edit invalidates approval.

loop.trigger: Proposed daily 09:00 Riga review plus each new request or supplier change. Assign a run ID; inspect unfinished prior runs first. Refresh relevant inventory with suppliers; treat availability older than 24 hours as unverified, not bookable stock.
loop.make: s09 would match dates including cleaning turnaround, item counts and collection area. Create a versioned draft showing rental, deposit, cleaning, transport, cancellation and proposed €3 separately. Use request ID + supplier ID + date range + quote version as the outbox deduplication key.
loop.check: s20 would independently compare supplier confirmation with requested quantities, dates, existing holds and all charges/terms. Reject missing or stale fields. Require supplier reconfirmation before reservation; only the ledger owner may allocate a hold, preventing concurrent double allocation.
loop.deliver: After checker approval, send one quote per outbox key through consented email. Record send time and status. Organiser acceptance is not a booking: supplier must confirm a reference and hold expiry. Request both parties' completion confirmation before marking completed or proposing a fee.
loop.exceptionOwner: s09 would own stale stock, disputes, missed runs and delivery failures. Retry supplier contact once after 24 hours; expire after 48 hours. For ambiguous email sends, inspect Sent before retrying. Freeze conflicting holds, notify affected parties, and escalate disputed terms to s20; never promise a refund or inventory without authority.

weeks.goal: Test sourcing pain and fee preference before building.
tasks: Prepare consent wording, request brief and direct-versus-assisted comparison; seek group moderator permission.
Seek two supplier listing permissions and written dated quantities, prices, deposits, cleaning, delivery and cancellation terms.
Run the ten-organiser invitation test within €20; log distinct responses and fee choices without collecting payment.
Stop or revise if supplier verification or demand thresholds fail; do not treat quote interest as purchase validation.

weeks.goal: If discovery passes, prepare the smallest controlled workflow.
tasks: Configure the private ledger, form and manual outbox; document permissions and deletion procedure.
Define requested, drafted, checked, sent, accepted, supplier-confirmed, completed, cancelled and expired states.
Assign s09 as operator/exception owner and s20 as independent checker; block self-approval.
Use synthetic records to rehearse stale availability, overlapping holds, changed quotes, duplicate intake and uncertain sends.

weeks.goal: Propose a bounded, human-run quote pilot.
tasks: Only with consent, process up to five dated requests using daily inventory refresh and checker sign-off.
Compare assisted coordination with direct booking and venue provision; log organiser reasons and human minutes.
Reconfirm supplier availability before any reservation; record supplier booking reference rather than claiming automatic booking.
Keep payments outside this pilot; record stated €3 preference separately from any future paid conversion.

weeks.goal: Review reliability, repeat intent and economic feasibility.
tasks: Audit every quote against supplier evidence and every send against its deduplication key.
Ask consenting organisers about their next event and preferred route; count a dated repeat request separately from general enthusiasm.
Calculate handling time, acquisition spend and hypothetical contribution; include cancellations and disputes.
Choose stop, narrow or continue. Automate reminders only if the manual loop passes; defer marketplace and payment development.

economics.hypothesis: The proposed €3 completion fee might support lightweight coordination only if handling time and acquisition costs are very low. Fee preference, completion, repeat usage and revenue remain unvalidated.
economics.costAssumptions: Planning assumptions: €20 total discovery budget, €12/hour operator opportunity cost and €0.30 per completion contingency for tools/administration. No payment processor selected; its fees remain unknown. Cloudflare's supplied $5/month paid minimum is an alternative cost, not required MVP spending.
economics.unitEconomics: Illustration, not results: €3 minus 5 minutes at €12/hour (€1) minus €0.30 leaves €1.70 before acquisition, payment fees, tax and disputes. At 15 minutes, contribution is -€0.30 before those costs. If €20 acquired three eventual completions, €6.67 acquisition cost each would exceed the fee.
unknowns: Actual supplier rental prices, deposits and liability allocation.
Completion rate, accepted paid fee, repeat frequency and acquisition cost.
Human minutes including checking, failed matches and disputes.
Payment collection costs, tax treatment, refunds and who bears cancellation losses.

tests.hypothesis: NGO organisers prefer €3 assistance over direct booking for dated needs.
tests.test: Human invites ten organisers after obtaining two permissioned, verified listings; presents comparable assisted, direct and venue options with all known charges. No payment collected.
tests.pass: Within seven days, three distinct organisers request dated quotes and at least two explicitly prefer assistance at €3.
tests.fail: Either threshold is missed, two verified listings cannot be obtained, or interest disappears when the fee is disclosed. Revise or stop; do not infer paid conversion.

tests.hypothesis: The separate checker and ledger prevent unsafe or duplicate releases.
tests.test: Human runs eight synthetic cases: stale stock, short quantity, missing cleaning term, date overlap, duplicate request, repeated send, changed approved quote and missed daily run.
tests.pass: All unsafe drafts are blocked; no duplicate send or conflicting allocation occurs; every case has an owner and auditable outcome.
tests.fail: Any unsafe release, duplicate send, conflicting hold or unowned exception. Repair and rerun before any external quote pilot.

tests.hypothesis: Assisted quotes can be reliable with little enough human work for a €3 fee.
tests.test: After earlier gates pass, time up to five consented requests, including preparation, checking, follow-up and failure handling; independently audit all sent quotes.
tests.pass: At least three quotes delivered, every quote verified, and average total handling at most five minutes per processed request. Treat this as a provisional threshold, not profitability proof.
tests.fail: Any unverified quote or average handling above five minutes; simplify, change the price hypothesis or stop rather than automate the loss.

risks: Municipal reuse guidance supports relevance, not demand for an intermediary.
Suppliers may decline listing permission or be unable to provide reliable dated inventory.
Direct supplier booking or venue stock may dominate the assisted option.
Cleaning, breakage, delivery and deposit disputes may overwhelm a €3 fee.
A spreadsheet hold is not a supplier reservation; stale confirmations can cause double booking.
Role separation requires two available humans; without a checker, quotes must wait.
unknowns: No customer contact, test, user activity, payment, deployment or implementation has occurred.
Which NGO organisers have recurring unmet needs and authority to pay?
Can two suppliers supply permissioned listings with complete dated terms?
What contractual, privacy and consumer obligations would apply before paid operation?
Would organisers return for another dated event rather than bypass the service?

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
